lesson.title: Lockdown Nation: America's Response to COVID-19
lesson.summary: The COVID-19 pandemic, declared a global emergency in March 2020, triggered an unprecedented federal, state, and scientific mobilization in the United States and became one of the most politically divisive issues in recent memory.
lesson.body:
COVID-19, caused by the novel coronavirus SARS-CoV-2, was first identified in Wuhan, China, in late 2019. The World Health Organization declared it a public health emergency of international concern on January 30, 2020, and a global pandemic on March 11, 2020. The United States confirmed its first known case in late January 2020, and the virus spread rapidly across the country over the following weeks, overwhelming some hospital systems and prompting an unprecedented peacetime disruption of American life.

The federal response unfolded during the final year of Trump's presidency. Trump declared a national emergency on March 13, 2020, freeing up federal resources, and Congress passed the CARES Act later that month, a roughly 2.2 trillion dollar package that expanded unemployment benefits, sent direct payments to most Americans, and provided loans to businesses through the Paycheck Protection Program. Because the Constitution gives states significant authority over public health, the most visible day to day decisions, stay at home orders, business and school closures, and later mask mandates, were made mostly at the state and local level, which meant the response varied considerably from state to state and sometimes became a point of political contrast, for example between more restriction focused states like California and New York and less restriction focused states like Florida and Texas.

On the scientific side, the Trump administration launched Operation Warp Speed in 2020, a public private partnership that funded and coordinated the development, manufacturing, and distribution of COVID-19 vaccines at a pace far faster than previous vaccine development had achieved. The Food and Drug Administration granted emergency use authorization to the Pfizer BioNTech vaccine and the Moderna vaccine in December 2020, and distribution continued to expand through 2021 under the Biden administration, which took office in January 2021.

The pandemic became one of the most politically divisive issues in recent American history. Mask wearing, business and school closures, and later vaccination itself all became associated with political identity for many Americans, with surveys consistently showing large gaps between Democrats and Republicans in support for various restrictions and in vaccine uptake. Public health officials and elected leaders disagreed at times over the right balance between limiting the virus's spread and limiting economic and social harm from restrictions, disagreements that were often amplified by the same social media dynamics discussed elsewhere in this unit. By official government counts, more than one million Americans died from COVID-19 over the course of the pandemic, one of the largest death tolls of any country, though public health researchers have noted that exact figures involve some counting challenges and have been refined over time. The pandemic left lasting effects on the American economy, workplace norms such as remote work, and public trust in health institutions and government at every level.
